summary:
This is the opening page of **chapter 4, "Classification and regression"** (PDF pages 128-159).

**This chapter covers:** your first examples of real-world machine learning workflows; handling binary and categorical classification problems; handling continuous regression problems.

The introduction says the chapter will consolidate what you learned in chapters 2 and 3 by applying it to three tasks that span the **three most common use cases** of neural networks:

- **Binary classification:** classifying movie reviews as positive or negative (section 4.1, IMDb, p.130).
- **Categorical (multiclass) classification:** classifying newswires by topic (section 4.2, Reuters, p.140).
- **Scalar regression:** estimating the price of a house from real-estate data (section 4.3, California Housing Price dataset, p.150).

These examples are your first contact with **end-to-end workflows**: data preprocessing, basic model architecture principles and model evaluation. Use this page as a roadmap: each section follows the same pattern (dataset, preparing the data, building the model, validating the approach, generating predictions, wrapping up), so you can compare how each choice changes with the problem type.

paragraphs.excerpt: This chapter is designed to get you started with using neural
paragraphs.what_it_says: The chapter gets you solving real problems with neural networks, consolidating chapters 2 and 3, through three tasks covering binary classification, categorical classification and scalar regression.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The three tasks differ mainly in what the target is: one of two classes, one of many classes, or a continuous number. That difference drives the choice of last-layer activation, loss and metric.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Most practical supervised problems fall into one of these three types, so learning the recipe for each covers a large share of real use cases.

paragraphs.why_it_matters: These three stages recur in every later project; chapter 6 generalises them into a universal workflow.

deeper.title: What changes between the three problem types
deeper.body:
Beyond this page (it is developed in the chapter itself): the usual last-layer/loss pairings are

| problem | last layer | loss |
|---|---|---|
| binary classification | 1 unit, sigmoid | binary crossentropy |
| categorical classification | N units, softmax | categorical crossentropy |
| scalar regression | 1 unit, no activation | mean squared error |

Keep this table in mind as a preview to check against sections 4.1-4.3.
